ATOD: Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation for Multi-turn Autonomous Agents

Qitai Tan Affiliation: Tencent Inc. Affiliation: Tsinghua University Email: tqt24@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn    Zefang Zong Affiliation: Tencent Inc. Email: willzong@tencent.com    Yang Li Affiliation: Tencent Inc. Email: thomasyngli@tencent.com    Peng Chen Affiliation: Tencent Inc.
Abstract

Training small language-model agents for long-horizon interactive tasks requires both fast imitation and reward-driven improvement. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense teacher guidance and typically improves rapidly in the early stage, but its gains saturate once the student approaches the teacher, limiting the final performance ceiling. Reinforcement learning (RL) directly optimizes environment rewards and encourages exploratory improvement toward a higher reward-defined ceiling, but sparse and delayed feedback makes early-stage learning much less efficient than OPD. In this paper, we propose ATOD (Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation), a hybrid online distillation algorithm that explicitly exploits this complementarity. (1) ATOD uses an annealed OPD–RL schedule: OPD dominates early training to approach teacher-level behavior, while RL is gradually strengthened to drive reward-based exploration. (2) ATOD introduces Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting (T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR}), which softly amplifies high-utility turns and improves dense supervision in long trajectories. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA show that ATOD consistently outperforms competing post-training baselines: across the three student sizes, ATOD improves average success rate by 3.03 points over OPD and 23.62 points over GRPO, while surpassing the corresponding teacher models by 2.16 points.

1 Introduction

Language agents extend large language models from static text generation to interactive decision making, where models must observe states, choose actions, call tools, and revise plans over multiple turns [1, 2]. Such capabilities make LLMs applicable to embodied instruction following, web shopping, search-augmented question answering, code execution, and other real-world tasks [3, 4, 5]. However, strong agentic behavior is usually concentrated in large models, whose inference cost and deployment overhead are undesirable in latency-, privacy-, and resource-sensitive settings. A practical goal is therefore to transfer multi-turn agentic competence from a stronger teacher to a smaller student, while still enabling the student to seek reward-driven improvements beyond pure teacher imitation.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has been widely used for post-training language agents. It optimizes the policy with environment-defined rewards, typically through PPO- or GRPO-style policy optimization [6, 7, 8, 9], with recent agent-oriented variants adapting this idea to long-horizon interaction [10, 11, 12, 13]. More recently, on-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as another promising paradigm: it trains the student on its own sampled trajectories while using a stronger teacher’s token-level distribution as dense supervision [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19].

However, RL and OPD exhibit complementary trade-offs in multi-turn agent training. RL directly pursues environment rewards and can improve beyond imitation, but sparse delayed feedback makes early exploration inefficient for small students. OPD provides dense token-level guidance and bootstraps learning quickly, but strong imitation can plateau near the teacher and suppress reward-improving deviations. This motivates an annealed OPD–RL schedule: OPD dominates early training to approach teacher-level behavior, while RL is gradually strengthened to drive reward-based exploration. The validation dynamics in figure 2(a) illustrate this complementarity: OPD improves quickly but saturates, GRPO grows slowly under sparse rewards, and the annealed hybrid preserves the fast start while reaching a higher ceiling.

A second challenge concerns where dense teacher supervision should be applied within long agent trajectories. In multi-turn agent tasks, different turns can have very different learning value: prior agentic OPD studies show that inter-turn error compounding can push later states outside the teacher’s reliable support, making uniform trajectory-level supervision unstable, and that distillation strength should be adapted at the step level [20, 21]. Meanwhile, token-importance studies in OPD suggest that student uncertainty and teacher–student disagreement identify informative distillation positions [22, 16]. We therefore lift this idea from tokens to turns, because a turn is the natural decision unit of an agent trajectory. As visualized in figure 2(b), entropy and disagreement vary substantially across turns; T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} estimates these signals from the log-probabilities of sampled tokens, avoiding full-vocabulary teacher sampling while efficiently assigning larger OPD weights to high-utility decision turns.

We propose ATOD, short for Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation, to address these two challenges with an annealed OPD–RL schedule and Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting (T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR}), as illustrated in figure 3. Together, these components improve early convergence, stabilize dense supervision, and raise the reward-driven performance ceiling. Our contributions are three-fold:

  • •

    We introduce an annealed OPD–RL training objective for multi-turn agent training. By letting OPD dominate early and RL dominate later, ATOD addresses the cold-start inefficiency of sparse-reward RL while preserving reward-driven improvement beyond pure teacher imitation.

  • •

    We propose Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting (T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR}), a soft distillation weighting mechanism for agentic OPD. T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} estimates turn-level distillation utility from student uncertainty and teacher–student disagreement, reducing wasted supervision on routine turns and emphasizing high-value decision points.

  • •

    We validate ATOD on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA across multiple student sizes. ATOD consistently outperforms competing post-training baselines, improves over both OPD and GRPO, and can surpass the corresponding teacher models.

2 Related Work

Language agents and tool-integrated reasoning.

Language agents combine reasoning with action, enabling LLMs to interact with tools, environments, and external feedback [1, 2]. Benchmarks such as ALFWorld, WebShop, and search-augmented QA require multi-step decision making under partial observations and delayed rewards [3, 4, 5]. These settings differ from single-turn text generation because errors can propagate across turns and because many actions are routine while a few are decisive.

Reinforcement learning for language models.

Policy optimization methods, including PPO and GRPO, have been widely used to improve language-model reasoning and alignment [6, 7, 8, 9]. Agent-specific RL methods further address long-horizon interaction through hierarchical multi-turn optimization, online curricula, group-in-group credit assignment, and adaptive exploration [10, 11, 12, 13]. GRPO is attractive because it estimates relative advantages within sampled groups without requiring a separate value model. However, in long-horizon agent tasks, sparse terminal rewards and high-variance exploration can make pure RL inefficient, especially for small models.

On-policy distillation.

OPD trains the student on its own generated trajectories while using a teacher distribution as dense supervision [14, 15]. This reduces the train–test mismatch of offline supervised distillation and improves sample efficiency. Recent OPD variants improve stability, context transfer, entropy handling, or teacher-ceiling behavior [16, 18, 17, 19]. For tool-using or multi-turn agents, recent work has explored step-wise, temporal, self-distilled, skill-conditioned, or importance-aware distillation to mitigate unreliable or redundant teacher signals [21, 20, 23, 24, 25, 22]. ATOD is complementary: it combines OPD with reward-driven GRPO through a dynamic schedule and uses T-DUR to softly gate only the distillation component.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Multi-Turn Agent Trajectories

We consider post-training a small language-model agent for multi-turn interactive tasks. Given an input xx, the student policy πθ\pi_{\theta} interacts with external feedback over KK steps. At step kk, the model generates a response aka_{k}, which may contain reasoning, an environment action or tool invocation, or a final answer. If an external action is taken, an observation oko_{k} is appended to the context and conditions subsequent generations.

A trajectory is defined as

τ=(x,a1,o1,…,aK,oK,aK+1),\tau=(x,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{K},o_{K},a_{K+1}), (1)

where aK+1a_{K+1} denotes the final response. The policy generates only model tokens, while observations are provided by the environment. Let ata_{t} denote a generated token and sts_{t} its prefix context, which may include both previous model outputs and environment observations.

3.2 Group Relative Policy Optimization

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a reinforcement learning algorithm that updates the policy using relative rewards within a group of sampled trajectories [7]. We assume access to an outcome-level reward function R⁡(τ)R(\tau) defined on complete trajectories. For each input xx, a group of trajectories {τi}i=1G\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} is sampled from the old policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, each receiving reward ri=R⁡(τi)r_{i}=R(\tau_{i}). The group-relative advantage is computed as

A^iGRPO=ri−mean⁡({rj}j=1G)std⁡({rj}j=1G)+ϵA.\hat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}=\frac{r_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})}{\mathrm{std}(\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G})+\epsilon_{A}}. (2)

Let

ηi,t​(θ)=πθθ​(ai,t∣si,t)πθold​(ai,t∣si,t)\eta_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}^{\theta}(a_{i,t}\mid s_{i,t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_{i,t}\mid s_{i,t})} (3)

denote the token-level importance ratio. The GRPO objective is

ℒGRPO​(θ)=−𝔼x​[1G​∑i=1G1|𝒯i|​∑t∈𝒯imin⁡(ηi,t​(θ)​A^iGRPO,clip⁡(ηi,t​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​A^iGRPO)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{i}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}\min\left(\eta_{i,t}(\theta)\hat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}},\;\mathrm{clip}(\eta_{i,t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}\right)\right], (4)

where 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} denotes the model-generated token positions in trajectory τi\tau_{i}. Equivalently, each generated token in τi\tau_{i} receives AtGRPO=A^iGRPOA_{t}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}=\hat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}. This objective provides an on-policy learning signal based on relative trajectory performance, but it relies on sparse outcome-level rewards.

3.3 On-Policy Distillation

On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training paradigm that provides dense token-level supervision on student-generated trajectories by aligning the student policy with a frozen teacher distribution [14, 15]. Given trajectories {τi}i=1G\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} sampled from the old student policy, the OPD objective can be written as

ℒOPD​(θ)=𝔼x​[1G​∑i=1G1|𝒯i|​∑t∈𝒯iηi,t​(θ)​(log⁡πθθ​(ai,t∣si,t)−log⁡πT​(ai,t∣si,t))],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{i}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}\eta_{i,t}(\theta)\left(\log\pi_{\theta}^{\theta}(a_{i,t}\mid s_{i,t})-\log\pi_{\mathrm{T}}(a_{i,t}\mid s_{i,t})\right)\right], (5)

where 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} denotes the model-generated token positions in trajectory τi\tau_{i}, and ηi,t​(θ)\eta_{i,t}(\theta) is the same importance ratio as in equation 3. This objective is a sampled estimator of the reverse KL divergence from the student policy to the teacher policy on student-visited states.

Equivalently, for a generated token ata_{t}, OPD provides the token-level distillation signal

Δ​log⁡pt=log⁡πT​(at∣st)−log⁡πθ​(at∣st),\Delta\log p_{t}=\log\pi_{\mathrm{T}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})-\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}), (6)

which is positive when the teacher assigns higher probability to the sampled token than the student. In advantage form, pure OPD uses

AtOPD=Δ​log⁡pt.A^{\mathrm{OPD}}_{t}=\Delta\log p_{t}. (7)

4 Method

4.1 Overview

ATOD combines two complementary learning signals. The teacher provides dense token-level guidance through OPD, which is especially useful when the student is still weak. The environment reward provides the task-defining signal through GRPO, which is essential for correcting teacher bias and improving beyond imitation. Instead of choosing one signal, ATOD uses both in a single token-level advantage:

At=κ⁡(s)​AtOPD+ρ⁡(s)​AtGRPO,\boxed{A_{t}=\kappa(s)\,A^{\mathrm{OPD}}_{t}+\rho(s)\,A^{\mathrm{GRPO}}_{t},} (8)

where

AtOPD=Δ​log⁡pt​wk⁡(t)=(log⁡πT​(at∣st)−log⁡πθ​(at∣st))​wk⁡(t).A^{\mathrm{OPD}}_{t}=\Delta\log p_{t}\,w_{k(t)}=\left(\log\pi_{\mathrm{T}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})-\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})\right)w_{k(t)}. (9)

Here ss is the global training step, and k⁡(t)k(t) maps token position tt to the turn that contains it. The coefficient κ⁡(s)\kappa(s) controls how much the update follows the teacher, while ρ⁡(s)\rho(s) controls how much it follows the environment reward. The scalar wk⁡(t)w_{k(t)} is the T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} weight of token tt’s turn. It only reweights the OPD term, so it changes where teacher supervision is applied without weakening the reward signal. The actor is then optimized with the same clipped surrogate as GRPO in equation 4, using AtA_{t} as the advantage. We do not add an explicit KL penalty; the teacher effect is already included through AtOPDA^{\mathrm{OPD}}_{t}.

4.2 Dynamic OPD/RL Coefficient Annealing

A fixed OPD/RL mixture is suboptimal because the two signals are useful at different stages. Early in training, rewards are sparse and noisy, while teacher guidance quickly teaches the student valid actions and interaction patterns. Later, pure imitation becomes limiting: the student may inherit teacher mistakes and cannot easily exceed the teacher. Therefore, ATOD gradually shifts the update from teacher-guided learning to reward-guided learning.

We use a simple progress variable

p⁡(s)=min⁡(sT,1),T=coef_anneal_steps,p(s)=\min\left(\frac{s}{T},1\right),\qquad T=\texttt{coef\_anneal\_steps}, (10)

which increases from 00 to 11 during the annealing window. The OPD coefficient is decreased as training progresses:

κ⁡(s)=max⁡(κmin,κinit−(κinit−κmin)​p​(s)),\kappa(s)=\max\left(\kappa_{\min},\;\kappa_{\mathrm{init}}-(\kappa_{\mathrm{init}}-\kappa_{\min})p(s)\right), (11)

and the RL coefficient is increased at the same time:

ρ⁡(s)=ρinit+(ρmax−ρinit)​p​(s).\rho(s)=\rho_{\mathrm{init}}+(\rho_{\max}-\rho_{\mathrm{init}})p(s). (12)

Intuitively, early updates keep κ⁡(s)\kappa(s) high, so the teacher provides a strong learning signal when reward feedback is still sparse. Late updates reduce the teacher weight and increase ρ⁡(s)\rho(s), so task reward becomes dominant. The floor κmin>0\kappa_{\min}>0 keeps a weak teacher anchor to reduce severe drift or reward hacking, but does not prevent reward-driven improvement.

4.3 Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting

For each turn kk, T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} computes two sampled-token statistics over response tokens.

Disagreement proxy.

dk=1Nk​∑t=1Nk|log⁡πθ​(at(k)∣st(k))−log⁡πT​(at(k)∣st(k))|.d_{k}=\frac{1}{N_{k}}\sum_{t=1}^{N_{k}}\left|\log\pi_{\theta}(a^{(k)}_{t}\mid s^{(k)}_{t})-\log\pi_{\mathrm{T}}(a^{(k)}_{t}\mid s^{(k)}_{t})\right|. (13)

A high dkd_{k} indicates strong student–teacher disagreement on the turn.

Uncertainty proxy.

hk=1Nk​∑t=1Nk(−log⁡πθ​(at(k)∣st(k))).h_{k}=\frac{1}{N_{k}}\sum_{t=1}^{N_{k}}\left(-\log\pi_{\theta}(a^{(k)}_{t}\mid s^{(k)}_{t})\right). (14)

This sampled-token negative log-probability estimates the student’s uncertainty over the turn.

Per-trajectory normalization.

For turns within the same trajectory τ\tau, we normalize

d~k=dk−minj∈τ⁡djmaxj∈τ⁡dj−minj∈τ⁡dj,h~k=hk−minj∈τ⁡hjmaxj∈τ⁡hj−minj∈τ⁡hj.\tilde{d}_{k}=\frac{d_{k}-\min_{j\in\tau}d_{j}}{\max_{j\in\tau}d_{j}-\min_{j\in\tau}d_{j}},\qquad\tilde{h}_{k}=\frac{h_{k}-\min_{j\in\tau}h_{j}}{\max_{j\in\tau}h_{j}-\min_{j\in\tau}h_{j}}. (15)

If the denominator is below 10−810^{-8}, the normalized value is set to 0.50.5. Per-trajectory normalization avoids mixing scales across tasks, trajectory lengths, and environment states.

Soft-OR fusion.

The final T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} turn weight is denoted by wkw_{k}:

wk=1−(1−d~k)​(1−h~k),wk∈[0,1].w_{k}=1-(1-\tilde{d}_{k})(1-\tilde{h}_{k}),\qquad w_{k}\in[0,1]. (16)

This continuous weight becomes large when either student–teacher disagreement or student uncertainty is high. Thus, it emphasizes both uncertain turns and low-uncertainty high-disagreement turns, the latter corresponding to cases where the student is confident but disagrees with the teacher. The detailed training procedure for ATOD is provided in algorithm 1 in Appendix A.1.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets & Benchmarks.

We evaluate ATOD on three long-horizon agent benchmarks: ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA. ALFWorld tests embodied instruction following in text-based household environments, WebShop evaluates goal-conditioned web navigation and product selection, and Search-QA measures search-augmented question answering over open-domain and multi-hop tasks [3, 4, 5]. Following common Search-R1-style protocols, the Search-QA suite covers Natural Questions, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle [26, 27, 28, 29, 30]. Together, these benchmarks cover embodied interaction, web interaction, and tool-assisted knowledge reasoning.

Evaluation Setups.

We use Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-4B as student models. The 0.6B and 1.7B students use a Qwen3-4B model trained with GRPO as the teacher, while the 4B student uses a Qwen3-30B-A3B GRPO teacher (150-step checkpoint). Unless otherwise specified, each prompt is sampled on policy with group size GG so that GRPO-style group-relative advantages can be computed from environment feedback. We report maximum validation success rate (%) and the corresponding average trajectory length on ALFWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop. The main comparison uses a 150-step training window for all student sizes.

Baselines.

We compare ATOD against post-training baselines of different supervision types: the untrained Vanilla model, the RL method GRPO, the self-distillation + RL method SDAR [25], standard on-policy distillation (OPD) [14, 15], and the agentic on-policy distillation methods SOD [21] and TCOD [20]. All methods use the same student and teacher families where applicable, and are evaluated under the same benchmark metrics. For ATOD, the teacher provides token-level log-probabilities on student-sampled trajectories, while the actor update remains the standard clipped GRPO surrogate with the hybrid advantage defined in equation 8. Baseline descriptions are provided in Appendix B.1.

5.2 Main Results

The performance comparison across ALFWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop is summarized in table 1, from which we draw the following key observations:

  • •

    Obs 1: ATOD consistently outperforms all baselines and even surpasses the corresponding teacher models. Across all three student sizes (0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B), ATOD achieves the highest average success rate among all student methods, with margins of 3.89% (0.6B), 5.07% (1.7B), and 2.13% (4B) over the second-best baseline. Notably, ATOD surpasses its teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop for all student sizes, and achieves competitive Search-QA performance within 1% of the teacher.

  • •

    Obs 2: ATOD delivers dramatic improvements for smaller models with weak initial performance. For the 0.6B student, which starts with near-zero success on ALFWorld (0.78%) and WebShop (4.69%), ATOD lifts performance to 82.81% and 86.72% respectively—a relative improvement of over 100×\times on ALFWorld compared to the vanilla model. In contrast, GRPO achieves only 30.47% on ALFWorld, highlighting ATOD’s superior efficiency in the early training stage when sparse rewards make pure RL ineffective.

5.3 Ablation Study

To evaluate the contribution of each component in ATOD, we conduct three ablation studies on ALFWorld across all student sizes (0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B): (1) applying the disagreement-uncertainty reweighting at the token level instead of the turn level (Token-level reweighting); (2) removing the T-DUR reweighting entirely and using uniform turn weights (w/o T-DUR); and (3) disabling the annealing schedule by fixing κ⁡(s)\kappa(s) and ρ⁡(s)\rho(s) to constant values (w/o Annealing). The results are shown in figure 4, from which we draw the following observations:

  • •

    Obs 1: The annealing schedule is crucial for combining imitation and reward optimization. Removing the annealing mechanism leads to the most pronounced degradation across all student sizes, with the largest drop on relatively weaker students (e.g., 0.6B drops from 82.8% to 75.8%). This confirms that a fixed OPD/RL mixture fails to balance the two signals effectively: early training requires strong teacher guidance for bootstrapping, while later training needs reward-driven pressure to push beyond the teacher ceiling.

  • •

    Obs 2: Turn-level T-DUR weighting outperforms both token-level reweighting and uniform weighting. Compared with ATOD, both applying reweighting at the token level and removing T-DUR (i.e., uniform turn weights) lower the success rate across all model sizes, with the gap being particularly notable on the 1.7B student. This suggests that operating at the turn level provides a more stable and semantically meaningful reweighting unit: agent interactions are inherently turn-structured, and aggregating disagreement and uncertainty over complete response turns better captures the utility of each decision step. In contrast, token-level reweighting introduces instability from per-token fluctuations, while uniform weighting squanders supervision on routine turns.

5.4 Training Dynamics and Diagnostic Metrics

figure 5 provides a step-wise view of the optimization process behind the aggregate results in table 1. Pure GRPO starts from a substantially lower success rate and improves slowly, reflecting the difficulty of exploration under sparse trajectory-level rewards. OPD and SOD obtain a much faster warm start because teacher supervision supplies dense token-level guidance, but their validation curves flatten after the early stage. In contrast, ATOD follows the rapid early growth of distillation-based methods while continuing to improve in the later stage, reaching the highest validation success rate by the end of training. The reward curve shows a consistent pattern: ATOD maintains a higher mean critic reward than the baselines for most of training, indicating that the annealed schedule does not merely imitate the teacher but gradually shifts toward reward-improving behaviors. The average-turn curve further suggests that ATOD learns more efficient interaction policies: while GRPO keeps producing longer trajectories, ATOD quickly reduces the number of turns and remains close to the more stable distillation-based baselines.

The diagnostic metrics in figure 6 further explain why the hybrid schedule is effective. The OPD signal is large at the beginning, when the student disagrees strongly with the teacher and dense supervision is most informative, but it quickly decreases as the student becomes aligned on common trajectory turns. This decay prevents teacher imitation from dominating indefinitely. Meanwhile, the RL signal increases early and remains high throughout training, providing persistent task-level pressure after the distillation signal weakens. The mean turn weight remains in a moderate range rather than collapsing, indicating that T-DUR continues to redistribute distillation strength across informative turns. The teacher–student gap also steadily shrinks for ATOD, confirming that the student absorbs useful teacher behavior while the persistent RL signal supplies the later reward-driven updates needed to exceed the ceiling of pure imitation.

6 Conclusion

We presented ATOD, an annealed turn-aware on-policy distillation algorithm for language agents. ATOD addresses the cold-start inefficiency of pure RL, the teacher-ceiling problem of pure OPD, and the signal dilution caused by uniform turn weighting. By encoding OPD and GRPO into a single hybrid advantage, annealing their coefficients over training, and applying T-DUR only to teacher supervision, the method provides a simple and implementation-friendly path toward training small agents that first imitate and then improve through environment reward.

Appendix A Method and Algorithmic Details

This section collects the implementation-level and analytical details of ATOD that complement the main method section.

A.1 Complete Training Algorithm

The complete ATOD training procedure is detailed below.

A.2 Gradient Interpretation of the OPD Component

Inside the unclipped region where ηt​(θ)≈1\eta_{t}(\theta)\approx 1, the distillation part of the actor loss is approximately

ℒOPD​(θ)≈−𝔼t​[ηt​(θ)​κ​(s)​Δ​log⁡pt​wk⁡(t)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta)\approx-\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\eta_{t}(\theta)\kappa(s)\Delta\log p_{t}w_{k(t)}\right]. (17)

Treating Δ​log⁡pt\Delta\log p_{t} and the turn weight wk⁡(t)w_{k(t)} as detached advantages, the gradient is

∇θℒOPD≈−𝔼t​[κ⁡(s)​Δ​log⁡pt​wk⁡(t)​∇θ​log​πθθ​(at∣st)].\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}\approx-\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\kappa(s)\Delta\log p_{t}w_{k(t)}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}^{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})\right]. (18)

Thus ATOD performs advantage-weighted likelihood ascent on student-sampled tokens, where the OPD advantage is high when the teacher assigns higher probability than the old student and T-DUR assigns a large disagreement-uncertainty weight to the turn.

A.3 Entropy Proxy as a Martingale-Difference Estimator

Claim 1.

For a turn kk, hk=1Nk∑t−logπθ(at(k)∣st(k))h_{k}=\frac{1}{N_{k}}\sum_{t}-\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}^{(k)}\mid s_{t}^{(k)}) is an unbiased estimator of the average token entropy H¯k=1Nk∑tH(πθ(⋅∣st(k)))\bar{H}_{k}=\frac{1}{N_{k}}\sum_{t}H(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}^{(k)})). Its estimation variance decreases at rate O⁡(1/Nk)O(1/N_{k}).

Proof sketch.

Let Xt=−log⁡πθ​(at∣st)X_{t}=-\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}) and let ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} be the filtration generated by previous tokens. Since at∼πθ(⋅∣st)a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}), we have 𝔼[Xt∣ℱt−1]=H(πθ(⋅∣st))\mathbb{E}[X_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=H(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})). Therefore Dt=Xt−HtD_{t}=X_{t}-H_{t} is a martingale difference. For i<ji<j, 𝔼⁡[Di​Dj]=𝔼⁡[Di​𝔼​[Dj∣ℱj−1]]=0\mathbb{E}[D_{i}D_{j}]=\mathbb{E}[D_{i}\mathbb{E}[D_{j}\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}]]=0. Hence the variance of the turn average is Nk−2​∑t𝔼⁡[Dt2]=O⁡(1/Nk)N_{k}^{-2}\sum_{t}\mathbb{E}[D_{t}^{2}]=O(1/N_{k}).

A.4 Properties of Soft-OR and Annealing

The function f⁡(d,h)=1−(1−d)​(1−h)f(d,h)=1-(1-d)(1-h) is monotone in both arguments, symmetric, satisfies f⁡(d,0)=df(d,0)=d and f⁡(0,h)=hf(0,h)=h, and is at least as large as each individual signal. It is the standard probabilistic OR t-conorm, making it appropriate when either uncertainty or disagreement should mark a turn as important.

The annealing functions in equations 11 and 12 are Lipschitz in the training step with constants |κinit−κmin|/T|\kappa_{\mathrm{init}}-\kappa_{\min}|/T and |ρmax−ρinit|/T|\rho_{\max}-\rho_{\mathrm{init}}|/T. This avoids abrupt changes in advantage scale and makes the transition between imitation and reward optimization smooth.

A.5 Naming Rationale

We use ATOD as the primary method name to align with the naming convention of recent OPD-family methods such as SOD and TCOD. The name emphasizes the two main algorithmic ingredients: annealed OPD–GRPO training and turn-aware distillation weighting. The turn weighting module is named Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting (T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR}) to emphasize that its soft weight is estimated from sampled-token student–teacher disagreement and student uncertainty, rather than from a hard token-selection rule.

Appendix B Experimental Setup Details

This section collects the experimental details needed to reproduce and interpret the reported results: baseline definitions, training configuration, metric diagnostics, and environment prompts.

B.1 Baselines

We compare ATOD with a diverse set of baselines spanning no additional training, reinforcement learning, self-distillation, and teacher-based on-policy distillation. These baselines are chosen to reflect different supervision sources (environment rewards, self-generated targets, and external teacher distributions) and different signal granularities (trajectory-level rewards, token-level distillation, and temporally structured agent feedback).

  • •

    Initial. The base student model without any additional task-specific post-training. This baseline measures the zero-shot or instruction-tuned agentic capability of the underlying Qwen3 student before reinforcement learning or distillation.

  • •

    GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). A reinforcement learning baseline that optimizes the student directly with environment rewards [7]. For each input, GRPO samples a group of candidate trajectories, assigns each trajectory a scalar task reward, and normalizes rewards within the group to estimate relative advantages. It avoids training a separate value model, making it efficient for LLM post-training, but the reward is usually sparse and trajectory-level in multi-turn agent tasks, so all tokens in a trajectory receive relatively coarse credit.

  • •

    SDAR (Self-Distilled Agentic Reinforcement Learning). SDAR keeps RL as the primary optimization backbone and adds a gated self-distillation objective as an auxiliary signal [25]. Instead of relying on an external teacher, it uses the agent’s own high-quality behaviors or self-generated targets to provide additional token-level guidance. This can improve credit assignment when the self-distilled signal is reliable, but its effectiveness depends on whether the student can already generate sufficiently useful agent trajectories.

  • •

    OPD (On-Policy Distillation). OPD trains the student on trajectories sampled from the student itself while using an external teacher distribution to provide dense token-level supervision [14, 15]. Compared with offline supervised imitation, OPD reduces train–test mismatch because supervision is applied on the student’s own rollout states. However, pure OPD mainly imitates the teacher and does not directly optimize environment rewards, so it may saturate once the student approaches teacher-like behavior.

  • •

    SOD (Step-wise On-policy Distillation). SOD is an agent-oriented OPD method that adaptively adjusts distillation strength at different interaction steps [21]. It is designed for long-horizon tool-use or agent trajectories, where different steps may have different levels of reliability and learning value. By assigning step-wise distillation weights, SOD provides more structured teacher guidance than uniform OPD, but it still relies primarily on teacher-driven supervision.

  • •

    TCOD (Temporal Curriculum On-Policy Distillation). TCOD introduces a temporal curriculum for multi-turn OPD [20]. Rather than exposing the student to the full trajectory difficulty uniformly, it controls the trajectory depth or temporal range used for distillation so that the student learns agent behavior in a progressively structured manner. This curriculum can stabilize multi-turn distillation, but its performance depends on the chosen temporal schedule.

The 4B GRPO model is reported as a teacher reference in the main table. All teacher-based distillation baselines use the same teacher checkpoint where applicable, so differences among OPD, SOD, TCOD, and ATOD mainly come from how teacher supervision is weighted and combined with reward optimization.

B.2 Training Hyperparameters

We conduct training across three text-based interactive environments: ALFWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop. The training and core ATOD hyperparameters are summarized in table 2, while task-specific configurations are provided in table 3.

B.3 Metric Interpretation

Healthy training should show monotonically decreasing hybrid/kl_coef, monotonically increasing hybrid/rl_coef, early OPD/RL ratio above one and late ratio below one, stable actor entropy without abrupt collapse, and increasing task reward. T-DUR active ratio should be high in early and middle training and may decrease later as the student approaches the teacher on more trajectories.

Appendix C Qualitative Examples and Diagnostic Analyses

This section provides concrete rollouts and diagnostic visualizations that explain where T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} allocates teacher supervision in long trajectories.

C.1 Qualitative ALFWorld Example

figure 10 shows a complete successful trajectory produced by the ATOD-trained 1.7B student on an ALFWorld task.

C.2 Turn-level Case Studies

We include two compact case studies in figures 11 and 12 to visualize how T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} assigns turn-level distillation weights. In each panel, dkd_{k} and hkh_{k} are the raw, pre-normalization proxies for teacher–student disagreement and sampled-token student uncertainty, respectively, while wkw_{k} is the final Soft-OR turn weight after per-trajectory normalization. The ALFWorld trace is from a trained student; the WebShop trace uses a pre-distillation student so that the reasoning-rich error-and-recovery pattern remains visible, with metrics computed against the same teacher. The layout follows the qualitative diagnostic style in which the task context appears above a step-wise trace, and the most important weight column is highlighted.

Case-study Takeaway

Across both domains, T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} reallocates dense teacher supervision toward pivotal decision points rather than routine environment mechanics. In ALFWorld, entropy highlights open-ended search and route planning, while disagreement rescues a confident goal-completion turn. In WebShop, the combination of uncertainty and disagreement flags error-and-recovery behavior around size/color selection and purchase commitment. This supports the design choice of using a Soft-OR fusion rather than relying on either signal alone.

C.3 T-DUR Diagnostic Metrics on ALFWorld

As shown in figure 13, the dashed line in each panel indicates the number of evaluation trajectories available at each training step. We compare the diagnostic curves of the untrained (pre-training) and trained (post-training) 1.7B student to illustrate how T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} allocates supervision.

Untrained model. Before training, the model achieves very low accuracy and exhibits an average trajectory length of 47.91 turns, which approaches the experimental maximum of 50 steps. This indicates that most samples produce long yet incorrect trajectories that exhaust the step budget. Panel (a) reveals a large teacher–student disagreement gap in the first few turns, where the teacher provides strong corrective signals against the student’s erroneous actions. However, the gap progressively decays at later turns: as earlier mistakes accumulate into a long erroneous prefix, the teacher’s distribution becomes less informative for distinguishing corrective actions, causing the disagreement to weaken. Panel (b) shows that the entropy proxy remains around 0.1 with little variation throughout the trajectory, reflecting that the untrained student stays in a persistently uncertain and error-prone regime across all turns. Consequently, Panel (c) shows that T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} assigns higher weights to earlier turns and progressively lower weights to later turns. This pattern is well-motivated: when the prompt prefix gradually drifts due to accumulated errors, the learning value of later turns diminishes, and distillation effort should instead concentrate on the earlier turning points and steps where mistakes first arise.

Trained model. After ATOD training, the teacher–student disagreement gap drops substantially compared to the untrained case (Panel a), confirming effective knowledge transfer. The entropy proxy (Panel b) exhibits a clear two-phase pattern: entropy remains at a low value during the first approximately 20 steps, then rises beyond step 20. This aligns with the observation that the trained model achieves markedly higher accuracy, with most successful trajectories completing within 25 turns; on these successful trajectories the student is confident and entropy is low. For trajectories that extend beyond 20 steps, early deviations or errors have likely already occurred, causing the student’s uncertainty to increase at later positions. Correspondingly, Panel (c) shows that T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} assigns small weights to the earlier, more confident and correct turns, while up-weighting the later turns where the student exhibits higher confusion and requires stronger teacher correction. This asymmetric weighting strategy enables T​-​DUR\mathrm{T\text{-}DUR} to focus distillation capacity on problematic decision points rather than wasting supervision on routine turns the student has already mastered.
